storyboard.relationToPrevious: Follows the viewer picture.

storyboard.relationToPrevious: Follows the Ivy League title.

storyboard.relationToPrevious: Starts the career move.

storyboard.relationToPrevious: Contrasts the grit with the sleek office.

storyboard.relationToPrevious: Follows the roster with the stakes.
storyboard.addedInformation: The team is in conflict and close to breaking.

storyboard.relationToPrevious: Transitions to the playbook.

storyboard.addedInformation: The whiteboard shows the reporting lines that were removed.

storyboard.relationToPrevious: Describes the merge that follows the board exercise.
storyboard.addedInformation: The gap is between what the employee thinks matters and what the manager knows matters.

image.subject: A large strategy map pinned on an office wall with colored zones and arrows, seen from a desk in front of it

storyboard.claim: The manager's broader strategic view shows what truly matters.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A strategy map pinned on an office wall.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Explains the manager's side of the gap.
storyboard.addedInformation: The map contrasts with minor operational concerns.

left.label: EMPLOYEE'S LIST
left.subject: A small handwritten note reading cafeteria food and a tiny bug fix

right.label: MANAGER'S LIST
right.subject: A bold printed chart of a competitor's market share with a red arrow pointing up

storyboard.claim: An employee's minor item is contrasted with a manager's major strategic pivot.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Small handwritten note on one side, competitor chart on the other.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Gives a concrete example of the gap.
storyboard.addedInformation: The employee has not considered the competitor at all.

storyboard.claim: The manager has found a blind spot in the employee's prioritization.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Bold punchline text on a plain background.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Resolves the example.
storyboard.addedInformation: The diagnosis gives the coach something to act on.

storyboard.claim: Bill's one-on-one framework goes well beyond a list of ongoing work.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Text on a plain background.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Moves from the diagnosis to the framework.
storyboard.addedInformation: The sources detail the framework.

storyboard.claim: The host asks what else was on Bill's list.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Bold question on a plain background.
storyboard.onScreenText: WHAT ELSE WAS ON HIS LIST?
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Follows the framework statement.
storyboard.addedInformation: None; the question leads to the answer.

storyboard.claim: The first part of the framework covers job performance.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Two-item checklist on a plain background.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Answers the question about the list.
storyboard.addedInformation: Performance on job requirements is the first item.

image.subject: A stocky white-haired man in his sixties, warm and direct, wearing a plain open-collar shirt and a sport jacket, leaning across a desk and asking a question while an employee listens

storyboard.claim: Bill constantly asks whether the employee gets along with peers.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Bill leaning across a desk asking a question.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Adds the peer-focused part of the framework.
storyboard.addedInformation: He asks about the engineering lead and the marketing director.

image.subject: A manager in a dark blazer sitting at a desk with a colleague, the two talking earnestly about coaching their own team members

storyboard.claim: Bill also asks how employees coach their own direct reports.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Two managers talking at a desk.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Continues the framework's management part.
storyboard.addedInformation: Management and leadership is the second theme.

image.subject: A lightbulb sketched on a whiteboard beside a simple process flowchart with arrows looping back

storyboard.claim: Innovation means constantly evaluating systems to get better.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Lightbulb sketch beside a process flowchart.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Adds the third theme of the framework.
storyboard.addedInformation: The focus on peer relationships separates Bill's playbook.

image.subject: A tall wooden ladder leaning against a glass office wall in an empty corridor

storyboard.claim: Most corporate structures assume the key relationship is vertical, like a ladder.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A ladder against a glass office wall.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Introduces the contrast with peer relationships.
storyboard.addedInformation: The ladder is the usual assumption about relationships.

storyboard.claim: Bill believed horizontal peer bonds matter more than vertical ones.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Bold question on a plain background.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Sets up the answer about cross-functional work.
storyboard.addedInformation: None; the question leads to the answer.

image.subject: Two colleagues from different departments shaking hands in a bright open-plan office hallway

storyboard.claim: Real cross-functional work happens between peers.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Two colleagues shaking hands in a hallway.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Answers the question about why peers matter.
storyboard.addedInformation: A good coach probes to keep those lateral bonds strong.

left.label: MARKETING VP
left.subject: A man in a sport jacket turning away from a colleague in a cold office

right.label: PRODUCT VP
right.subject: An engineer with a laptop looking away from the manager across a desk

storyboard.claim: If two VPs dislike each other, the company eventually fails.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Two executives turned away from each other.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Gives the consequence of weak peer bonds.
storyboard.addedInformation: Liking the CEO does not compensate for the rift.

image.subject: A woman in her thirties with shoulder-length brown hair and a cardigan sitting back in her chair at a desk, waiting while a team member sits across from her

storyboard.claim: A new manager who only waits for the employee looks passive.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A manager sitting back in her chair, waiting.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Turns to the new manager's worry.
storyboard.addedInformation: The manager fears looking like they lack direction.

storyboard.claim: Sitting back and waiting for the employee to set the agenda looks passive to a new manager.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Text-only question card; the word PASSIVE carries the worry.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Picks up the new manager from the previous beat, now stuck in the one-on-one.
storyboard.addedInformation: Frames the objection the chapter will answer.

image.subject: A woman in her thirties with shoulder-length brown hair and a cardigan, sitting across a desk from a colleague, leaning back in her chair with a relaxed, uncertain look while the colleague talks.

storyboard.claim: A manager who waits for her report to steer the meeting seems to have lost control.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The manager leaning back at her desk while her colleague does the talking across from her.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Continues the new-manager worry as a visible scene.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the appearance of weakness the narration describes.

image.subject: A stocky white-haired man in his sixties, warm and direct, wearing a plain open-collar shirt and a sport jacket, the posture of a football coach, leaning forward across a table and listening closely to someone out of frame.

storyboard.claim: The strongest move in a one-on-one is listening, not dominating.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Bill Campbell leaning forward at a table, fully attentive.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Answers the worry: passivity is reframed as control.
storyboard.addedInformation: Introduces Campbell as the model for the listening coach.

storyboard.claim: Campbell's colleagues called it free form listening, and listening is power.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Text-only punchline card.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Names the technique from the previous line.
storyboard.addedInformation: Gives the technique its name, free form listening.

image.subject: A woman in her thirties with shoulder-length brown hair and a cardigan, sitting across a desk from a colleague, calmly watching the colleague who is thinking hard and drawing a plan on a notepad.

storyboard.claim: Letting the employee set the agenda lets the manager evaluate how they think.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The manager quietly observing a colleague who is working out a plan on paper.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Explains what the silence reveals.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the evaluation as an observed behaviour, not a metaphor.

storyboard.claim: Coaching how to think and prioritize beats handing over a to-do list.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Text list with three short steps set against the phrase TO-DO LIST.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Contrasts the coaching approach with simply assigning tasks.
storyboard.addedInformation: Lists the three things the employee learns to do.

image.subject: An engineer's desk with two monitors and a code editor open, a manager standing beside it with her hands in her pockets, not touching the keyboard.

storyboard.claim: The one-on-one is not for fixing code or copy, it is for developing the person.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A manager beside an engineer's workstation, hands off the keyboard.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Ties the previous point to the core thesis of the book.
storyboard.addedInformation: Makes the point concrete with a workstation.

image.subject: A young engineer in a casual sweater standing alone at a glass-walled office whiteboard, drawing a plan with confidence while a manager sits back in a chair across the room watching.

storyboard.claim: The goal is an employee who operates autonomously within the wider team.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The engineer working out a plan alone at the whiteboard while the manager watches.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Extends the workstation point to autonomy.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows autonomy as the engineer working without being told what to do.

image.subject: A glass-walled boardroom with a long conference table, six people seated around it in animated discussion, a whiteboard with diagrams behind them.

storyboard.claim: A business moves forward through collective decisions and group dynamics.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Six people in a boardroom debating around a long table.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Moves from one-on-ones to the group meeting.
storyboard.addedInformation: Sets the group setting for the rest of the chapter.

image.subject: A group of a dozen office workers in business clothes walking together into a glass-walled meeting room, folders and laptops in hand, the door held open by one of them.

storyboard.claim: Strong individuals must be gathered into one room to decide the company's future.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A dozen colleagues walking into the same meeting room together.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Brings the coached individuals into one room.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the size and mix of a leadership group.

storyboard.claim: What happens when the group is deadlocked on a critical issue?
storyboard.concreteVisual: Text-only question card.
storyboard.onScreenText: What happens when they are deadlocked?
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Turns from group dynamics to a specific tense case.
storyboard.addedInformation: Sets up the Google conference room scene.

image.subject: A man in his fifties with short graying hair and a dark blazer over an open-collar shirt, measured and attentive, seated at the head of a long conference table in a Google conference room, two empty chairs in front of him.

storyboard.claim: The scene takes place in Eric Schmidt's conference room at Google, under visible tension.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Eric Schmidt at the head of a long conference table with empty chairs.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Moves from the question to the scene location.
storyboard.addedInformation: Places Schmidt as the CEO managing the dispute.

image.subject: Two men in their forties in dark suits sitting at opposite ends of a long conference table, arms folded, both looking away from each other.

storyboard.claim: A bitter turf war has broken out between two senior executives.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Two executives at opposite ends of a table, arms folded, refusing to look at each other.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Describes the dispute set up in the scene.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the hostility as body language.

image.subject: A smartphone lying face up on a conference table, with two sets of hands reaching for it from opposite sides.

storyboard.claim: The two executives are fighting over who owns a massive new mobile app.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A phone on a table with two pairs of hands reaching for it from opposite sides.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Names the prize in the turf war.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the object at the centre of the dispute.

left.label: EXECUTIVE A
left.subject: A senior executive in a dark suit, jaw set, leaning toward the table with his finger raised to make a point.

right.label: EXECUTIVE B
right.subject: A senior executive in a dark suit, arms crossed, shaking his head and not moving forward in his chair.

storyboard.claim: Two big egos are colliding in the dispute.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Two executives in opposition, one leaning in and one refusing to yield.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Introduces the two sides of the feud.
storyboard.addedInformation: Contrasts the two egos side by side.

image.subject: Two men in suits walking side by side down a glass-walled office corridor toward a small meeting room, one carrying a laptop, the room door already open.

storyboard.claim: Schmidt sends the two feuding executives off to gather data and return with a compromise.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The two executives walking together toward a small room to work it out.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Shows Schmidt's diplomatic move.
storyboard.addedInformation: Names the rule Schmidt uses.

image.subject: A conference table with two laptops facing opposite ways, each screen showing a different chart, and no one reaching across to the other side.

storyboard.claim: The rule of two fails because both executives protect their own teams.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Two laptops turned away from each other on a table, each showing a rival chart.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Shows why the compromise approach is failing.
storyboard.addedInformation: Makes the entrenched positions visible.

image.subject: A stocky white-haired man in his sixties, warm and direct, wearing a plain open-collar shirt and a sport jacket, the posture of a football coach, sitting at the edge of a conference table and quietly watching a heated argument.

storyboard.claim: Bill Campbell sits in the room, watching the debate turn personal.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Campbell at the table's edge, silent and watching the argument.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Brings Campbell into the scene as the turning point.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows Campbell still and observant before he speaks.

storyboard.claim: Campbell cuts through the diplomacy and orders the two executives to break the tie.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Text-only quote card with the line set large.
storyboard.onScreenText: Either you two break that tie or I will cut the...
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Campbell speaks after the silent watching shown in the previous beat.
storyboard.addedInformation: Gives the exact line Campbell uses to force the decision.

storyboard.claim: That moment defines the manager's role in decision making.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Text-only punchline card.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Closes Campbell's ultimatum with the one-word verdict.
storyboard.addedInformation: States the lesson of the scene in one word.

storyboard.claim: Leaders are taught that getting everyone to agree is the mark of good leadership.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Text-only question card.
storyboard.onScreenText: Isn't getting everyone to agree the hallmark of leadership?
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Raises the common belief the book challenges.
storyboard.addedInformation: States the conventional view to be overturned.

image.subject: A manager at the head of a round conference table with five colleagues, each one speaking in turn, the manager sitting with open hands and listening.

storyboard.claim: You want an ensemble that feels heard, but the job is not to find consensus.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A round table of colleagues speaking in turn while the manager listens with open hands.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Answers the agreement question with a nuance.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the ensemble approach as the right way to gather ideas.

image.subject: A whiteboard in a glass office with a lukewarm compromise written on it in faded marker, a half-erased line and the marker set down on the tray.

storyboard.claim: Bill Campbell hated consensus because it produces watered-down compromises.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A whiteboard with a faded, compromised plan on it.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Explains why consensus is rejected.
storyboard.addedInformation: Makes the idea of a watered-down result physical.

left.label: OFFENDS THE FEWEST
left.subject: A cautious committee of five people nodding politely around a conference table, nobody pushing an idea.

right.label: OPTIMAL
right.subject: A single bold sketch on a whiteboard drawn by one engineer, bright and specific, with the marker still in hand.

storyboard.claim: Deciding to offend the fewest people rarely produces the best decision.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A polite committee on the left, one bold sketch on the right.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Explains the cost of consensus.
storyboard.addedInformation: Contrasts the safe decision with the innovative one.

image.subject: A manager at a glass whiteboard with a numbered checklist of steps, marker in hand, reviewing the steps with two colleagues seated nearby.

storyboard.claim: The manager's job is to run a rigorous process.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A manager at a whiteboard working through numbered steps with colleagues.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Turns the critique of consensus into the manager's real task.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the process as a visible checklist.

storyboard.claim: A rigorous process surfaces all dissent, lets the team debate, then the manager breaks the tie if needed.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Text list of three steps.
storyboard.onScreenText: SURFACE DISSENT / DEBATE FIERCELY / BREAK THE TIE
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Lists the steps of the process the previous beat named.
storyboard.addedInformation: Gives the sequence the manager follows.

image.subject: A manager at the head of a conference table pointing decisively at one of two printed proposals, nodding with a firm expression, the other proposal pushed aside.

storyboard.claim: When the team cannot align on the data, the manager breaks the tie without hesitation.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A manager pointing to one proposal and pushing the other aside.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Applies the final step of the process.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the decision as a physical act at the table.

storyboard.claim: How do you get every dissenting idea on the table before breaking the tie?
storyboard.concreteVisual: Text-only question card.
storyboard.onScreenText: How do you get the dissent on the table first?
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Asks for the specific mechanical rule behind the process.
storyboard.addedInformation: Leads into the Marissa Meyer example.

image.subject: A young woman executive in her thirties in a tailored blazer, seated at the head of a conference table with her hands folded, listening quietly.

storyboard.claim: Campbell gave a rising executive a strict, non-negotiable rule for running her team.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A young woman executive at the head of the table, hands folded, silent.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Introduces the example behind the mechanism.
storyboard.addedInformation: Puts the rule into a specific leader's meeting.

storyboard.claim: What was the rule Campbell gave her?
storyboard.concreteVisual: Text-only question card.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Sets up the answer the next beat reveals.
storyboard.addedInformation: Builds suspense before the rule is named.

storyboard.claim: The leader always speaks last.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Text-only punchline card.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Answers the question with the rule.
storyboard.addedInformation: States the rule in its shortest form.

image.subject: A young woman executive in a blazer at a conference table, mouth closed, holding a pen loosely, while colleagues around her speak and gesture.

storyboard.claim: Blurting out the answer at the start shuts down the conversation, even when the leader is right.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The leader holding back while others speak.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Explains why the rule matters for a brilliant leader.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows restraint from a leader who already knows the answer.

image.subject: A small team of four around a whiteboard, each adding a line to the same diagram, the marker passing from hand to hand.

storyboard.claim: Speaking last lets the team reach the answer together.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Four team members taking turns at a whiteboard diagram.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Shows the benefit of the rule in a team.
storyboard.addedInformation: Makes the collaborative process visible.

image.subject: A young team member holding a printed proposal and making a point with one raised finger, colleagues around the table nodding and taking notes.

storyboard.claim: The team exercises decision making by debating, analyzing and arguing its points.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A team member arguing with a proposal while colleagues take notes.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Describes what the team does when it is given room.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the argument as a healthy exchange.

image.subject: A row of silent team members sitting with their hands folded, all turned toward an empty chair at the head of a long table.

storyboard.claim: Without the rule, teams sit passively waiting for the leader to speak.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Team members looking at an empty chair at the head of the table.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Shows the failure the rule prevents.
storyboard.addedInformation: Makes the passive team physically visible.

storyboard.claim: In a fast-paced environment, speed is everything, so why should the leader hold back?
storyboard.concreteVisual: Text-only question card.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Raises the objection to speaking last.
storyboard.addedInformation: Sets up the crisis example.

image.subject: An engineer at a desk late at night with two monitors showing a red error log, a colleague leaning over her shoulder to look at the screen.

storyboard.claim: A critical bug crashing the servers seems to justify skipping the debate.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Two engineers at night looking at a red error log on monitors.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Gives the strongest version of the objection.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the urgent case in a real engineering setting.

image.subject: A stopwatch resting on a desk beside a printed chart of falling revenue, the chart's edge pressed under a coffee mug.

storyboard.claim: Debating the best solution for an hour seems to waste precious time and revenue.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A stopwatch and a falling revenue chart on a desk.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Adds the cost of the delay.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the cost of time as objects on the desk.

image.subject: A manager at a desk with a wall calendar, calmly circling a single date while a colleague looks on, the desk otherwise tidy.

storyboard.claim: Most daily tasks are not emergencies, so the false assumption is the problem.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A calm manager circling one date on a wall calendar.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Answers the objection by naming the false assumption.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the difference between an emergency and a normal day.

image.subject: A Silicon Valley office building at night with one floor lit and an orange emergency glow on the glass, an empty street below.

storyboard.claim: A real crisis, with servers down and a PR disaster unfolding, is a literal emergency.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A quiet office building at night with one floor lit by an emergency glow.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Concedes the objection a genuine emergency exists.
storyboard.addedInformation: Sets up the distinction the next line draws.

image.subject: A stern manager in a glass-walled office points at a whiteboard while three engineers stand in front of it, one of them giving a short nod

storyboard.claim: Command-and-control leadership means giving orders and executing them.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A manager directing a small team from the front of a whiteboard.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Opens the new idea that leadership styles differ by the kind of decision.
storyboard.addedInformation: The picture shows the directive style that suits urgent, top-down moments.

image.subject: A product team gathered around a conference table covered with printed charts and laptops, calmly weighing options with no sense of rush

storyboard.claim: Most corporate decisions are structural choices, not literal fires.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A calm team studying charts at a table, the opposite of an emergency.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Contrasts the fire metaphor from the previous beat with ordinary business decisions.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the everyday pace of a normal decision.

image.subject: Engineers debate across a long table while a manager sits back in a chair with arms folded, letting the discussion run

storyboard.claim: Letting the team debate is an investment in their ability.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A manager stepping back as the team argues over a design.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Follows the structural-choice idea with the cost of waiting to decide.
storyboard.addedInformation: The manager is absent from the argument, which is the point.

image.subject: A stocky white-haired man in his sixties, warm and direct, wearing a plain open-collar shirt and a sport jacket, sits at the edge of a conference table listening while a team presents at a whiteboard

storyboard.claim: Building a team means trusting the process to reach the best result.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Bill Campbell listening while others present.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Adds the team trust idea after the long-term investment point.
storyboard.addedInformation: Campbell is shown as the listener, not the decider.

storyboard.claim: Trust comes from knowing every voice is heard before the tie is broken.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Text-led statement, no picture needed.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Confirms the process point with a short agreement.
storyboard.addedInformation: Only a short confirmation, so no picture.

storyboard.claim: The hardest scenario is when the rigorous process gets hijacked.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Real question on screen.
storyboard.onScreenText: What happens when that rigorous process is hijacked?
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Turns from the process ideal to the problem case.
storyboard.addedInformation: Frames the next section as the difficult case.

image.subject: A young engineer in his late twenties leans back at a workstation with two monitors, looking self-assured while colleagues behind him glance away

storyboard.claim: A visionary team member can hijack the process.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A confident engineer at a desk, colleagues looking away.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Answers the question with a person, not an abstraction.
storyboard.addedInformation: Introduces the aberrant genius as an ordinary desk-level figure.

image.subject: A cluttered engineer's desk with a screen full of code, a half-empty coffee cup, and a chair pushed away from a neighboring desk

storyboard.claim: Someone brilliant but a nightmare to work with.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Brilliant code output and an empty chair beside it.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Gives the aberrant genius a name.
storyboard.addedInformation: The empty chair hints at the cost to colleagues.

storyboard.claim: Everyone has seen this person.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Text-led statement.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Speaker's aside before listing the archetypes.
storyboard.addedInformation: Rapport beat, no picture.

storyboard.claim: Three archetypes of the aberrant genius.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A real list of three roles.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Lists the types the previous beat named.
storyboard.addedInformation: Names three familiar roles in a tech company.

image.subject: A stocky white-haired man in his sixties, warm and direct, wearing a plain open-collar shirt and a sport jacket, sits across a desk from a frustrated woman in her thirties with shoulder-length brown hair and a cardigan, her hand pressed to her forehead

storyboard.claim: A frustrated manager sits with Bill defending a toxic genius.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Campbell listening across a desk from a worn-out manager.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Gives the scene from the list a real setting.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the emotional cost on the manager.

left.label: BRILLIANT WORK
left.subject: A laptop screen filled with clean, elegant code on a bright office desk

right.label: TOXIC TO TEAM
right.subject: Three colleagues sit silent at a conference table, eyes down, while one chair stands empty

storyboard.claim: The employee produces brilliant work but is toxic to people around them.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Two sides: the code and the silent team.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Explains why the manager struggles with the employee.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the two sides of the same person.

image.subject: A stocky white-haired man in his sixties, warm and direct, wearing a plain open-collar shirt and a sport jacket, leans forward in his chair listening intently to a manager who is talking with both hands

storyboard.claim: Bill listens closely while the manager makes the case.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Campbell leaning forward, attentive.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Continues the scene with Campbell's reaction.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows his listening style before his reply.

image.subject: A manager in a light blazer bends forward across a desk, gesturing toward a small stack of performance reviews

storyboard.claim: The manager bends over backward to justify keeping the employee.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A manager gesturing over reviews.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Describes the manager's effort from the previous beat.
storyboard.addedInformation: The reviews show the justification being made.

storyboard.claim: Bill asks how to keep the good and drop the bad.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Real quotation from Bill.
storyboard.onScreenText: How can we capture the good and dismiss the bad?
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Bill's reply to the manager.
storyboard.addedInformation: A direct quotation, shown as text.

image.subject: A cardboard box packed with personal items sits on an empty desk in a glass-walled office after a name plate has been removed

storyboard.claim: You cannot be with him 18 hours a day, and the genius was let go.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A packed box on an empty desk.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Shows the consequence of Bill's reply.
storyboard.addedInformation: The packed box shows the departure.

image.subject: A rumpled, eccentric engineer in a hoodie sketches on a whiteboard while colleagues around a table look on with patience

storyboard.claim: You tolerate the quirky and difficult because they drive innovation.
storyboard.concreteVisual: An eccentric engineer sketching while others are patient.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: States the rule after the story.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the tolerated eccentricity.

image.subject: A young engineer stands at a whiteboard working through a diagram alone while a colleague watches from a distance

storyboard.claim: Give them space until they cross into toxicity.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Engineer alone at a board, given room.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Adds the limit to the tolerance rule.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the space being granted.

storyboard.claim: Toxicity is when they break communication, scare colleagues, and drain management.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A real list of three warning signs.
storyboard.onScreenText: BROKEN TEAM COMMUNICATION / FEAR IN MEETINGS / ENDLESS DAMAGE CONTROL
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Defines the crossing point.
storyboard.addedInformation: Three concrete signs of the line.

image.subject: A manager closes the door of a glass-walled office, an empty chair facing the closed door

storyboard.claim: Once toxic, you have to cut them loose.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A closed office door with an empty chair.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Consequence of crossing the line.
storyboard.addedInformation: The door shows the separation.

storyboard.claim: What is the warning sign that a genius has gone too far?
storyboard.concreteVisual: Real question on screen.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Leads into the specific warning sign.
storyboard.addedInformation: Sets up the answer about fame.

image.subject: A glossy business magazine cover lies on a desk, showing a smiling executive in a crisp shirt, a camera flash reflecting on the glossy page

storyboard.claim: Bill strongly disliked executives who sought their own PR.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A magazine cover with a self-promoting executive.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Answers the warning-sign question.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the self-promotion Bill disliked.

image.subject: A founder in a dark blazer poses under camera flashes at a press event, a small crowd of photographers pressing forward

image.subject: an open desk calendar with one-on-one meetings blocked out in neat rows, a pen resting across the page

storyboard.claim: Bill Campbell is caught in the middle: friend to Jobs, adviser to Apple, mentor to Google.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Campbell standing between two empty chairs, caught in the middle.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Places Campbell in the middle of the two sides from the compare.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows his three roles as a position, not a list.

image.subject: A man in his fifties with short graying hair and a dark blazer over an open-collar shirt, leaning across a desk toward a stocky white-haired man in a sport jacket, speaking urgently

storyboard.claim: Eric Schmidt brings Bill the absolute legal and business problem.

storyboard.relationToPrevious: Brings the problem to Campbell, who is in the middle.

image.subject: A cluttered executive desk with patent folders, a stack of legal briefs and a open laptop showing dense text, a legal pad covered with notes

storyboard.claim: A CEO's instinct is to dive into the patents, the briefs and the lawyers.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A desk piled with patents, briefs and notes.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Describes the expected reaction Campbell does not have.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the detailed work the instinct would begin with.

image.subject: A closed stack of unread legal briefs sitting untouched on a clean glass office table, with a single pen placed neatly beside them

storyboard.claim: Campbell does not read a single patent or legal brief.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A closed stack of briefs left untouched on a clean table.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Shows what Campbell does not do, in contrast with the instinct.
storyboard.addedInformation: Makes the refusal to dive in a visible, untouched object.

kicker: PUT THE RIGHT PERSON IN CHARGE

image.subject: A stocky white-haired man in his sixties, warm and direct, wearing a plain open-collar shirt and a sport jacket, pointing decisively across a conference table toward a colleague who is listening

storyboard.claim: Campbell tells Schmidt to put Alan Eustace in charge of diplomacy between the two companies.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Campbell points across the table, directing the assignment.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Gives the concrete action that replaces diving into details.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the decision as a gesture of delegation.

image.subject: A pair of hands moving a single chessboard piece to a new square on a glass-topped office table, with a folder of papers pushed aside

storyboard.claim: Skipping the details is the operational pivot of a master manager.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A hand moves one piece while papers are pushed aside.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Explains why the delegation is a move, not an abdication.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows strategic repositioning as a single decisive move.

storyboard.claim: The first panicked instinct is to ask how to solve the problem.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Text-only question card.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Names the instinct the previous beats said to resist.
storyboard.addedInformation: The question is the one the reader is asked to stop asking.

image.subject: A manager in a cardigan with a hand raised toward her own face, pausing mid-thought at her desk, a closed notebook in front of her

storyboard.claim: You have to train yourself to stop before fixing.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A manager pauses with a hand raised, halting an impulse.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Turns the question into the act of stopping.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the pause as a physical act.

image.subject: A cluster of engineers leaning in together around one laptop at a workstation, two monitors glowing behind them, all talking at once

storyboard.claim: The correct question is who the right team is, not how to solve it.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Engineers gather around a laptop to work out the problem together.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Gives the replacement question a picture of a team.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows a team forming around the problem.

image.subject: A bright open office with a small group of colleagues seated together at a long table, facing one another rather than a single leader

storyboard.claim: You work with the team, not the problem.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A group seated around a table facing one another.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: States the principle the team picture illustrated.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the layout of equal peers.

image.subject: A group of six young associate product managers in an open Silicon Valley office, gathered around a table with laptops and notebooks, deep in a heated discussion

storyboard.claim: The associate product managers at Google are a group of very sharp young people.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Six young product associates at a table in a meeting.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Introduces the group in the example of the principle.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the size and youth of the group.

image.subject: Young associates slumped over a table covered in printed forms and a tangle of sticky notes, looking frustrated

storyboard.claim: The group is stuck on minor bureaucratic problems and technical roadblocks.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Frustrated young associates over paper forms and sticky notes.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Describes the group's complaints from the previous beat.
storyboard.addedInformation: Makes the minor obstacles look heavy.

image.subject: A woman in her thirties with shoulder-length brown hair and a cardigan, leaning over a colleague's laptop and reaching to take the keyboard, a confident look on her face

storyboard.claim: Marissa's instinct is to jump in and fix their problems herself.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A manager reaches over and takes the keyboard from a colleague.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Shows the instinct the APM group's complaints provoke.
storyboard.addedInformation: The keyboard grab shows the takeover as an action.

image.subject: A stocky white-haired man in his sixties, warm and direct, wearing a plain open-collar shirt and a sport jacket, speaking quietly with a hand on the wall of a bright corridor

storyboard.claim: Bill observes and pulls her aside to speak privately.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Campbell speaks quietly in a corridor.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Moves from the instinct to Campbell's intervention.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the private, one-to-one setting of the advice.

storyboard.claim: Campbell tells her she is entirely the wrong person to help them.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Text-only statement.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Delivers the counterintuitive verdict the aside led to.
storyboard.addedInformation: Sets up the reasons in the next beat.

image.subject: A corner office with a large desk and a high-backed leather chair, empty, seen from the doorway of a room where junior staff sit at small tables

storyboard.claim: She is their boss and knows the answer, but has too much institutional power.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A large corner office looking over smaller desks.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Explains why she is the wrong person.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the power gap as a physical distance.

image.subject: Two young professionals sitting together at a bright table with a whiteboard, a clear space at the head of the table left unoccupied

storyboard.claim: She should create a peer forum where the APMs can meet without her.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Peers at a table with the head seat left empty.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Gives the remedy for the power problem.
storyboard.addedInformation: The empty head of the table shows the manager stepping back.

image.subject: A circle of young professionals in folding chairs in a bright office, leaning in and speaking openly to one another, no manager at the center

storyboard.claim: The forum forces peer-to-peer vulnerability.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A circle of peers speaking openly.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Explains the effect of the peer forum.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the vulnerability as a circle with no authority at its center.

image.subject: A whiteboard covered in notes beside a young team tapping their own laptops and working out the next steps together, no manager hovering nearby

storyboard.claim: The team builds its own capacity instead of waiting for answers from a vending machine.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A team working through next steps at a whiteboard without a manager.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Contrasts self-solving with the vending machine the manager would have been.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the team solving on its own.

storyboard.claim: Banter that connects back to the burning building analogy from earlier.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Text-only statement.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Hosts transition between speakers.
storyboard.addedInformation: None beyond the callback.

storyboard.claim: Let's push back on the optics of this tactic.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Text-only question card.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Opens the counterargument.
storyboard.addedInformation: Frames the objection the next beats answer.

image.subject: A manager at a glass office table with arms folded, looking past an empty chair while a team works in the background

storyboard.claim: If the team is failing and the leader delegates without looking at details, it looks like passing the buck.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A manager with folded arms, distant from a working team.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: States the objection in concrete terms.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the detachment the objection warns about.

storyboard.claim: Passing the buck is what it looks like.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Text-only punchline.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Lands the objection.
storyboard.addedInformation: None beyond the phrase.

image.subject: A leader in shirtsleeves rolling up sleeves at an engineer's desk, leaning in to a monitor with colleagues gathered around, a visible wish to be part of the work

storyboard.claim: Getting in the trenches is a common misconception of good leadership.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A leader rolls up sleeves to join the work at a desk.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Gives the counter-view a face.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the misconception as a sincere, human impulse.

image.subject: A coiled red fire hose mounted on the wall of a glass-walled office corridor, with a closed door at the end

storyboard.claim: Grabbing the fire hose at executive level is micromanaging the fire.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A fire hose on a corridor wall, unused.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Gives the metaphor a literal object.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the metaphor's tool without any fire or harm.

storyboard.claim: If you keep jumping into technical trenches, you abandon your actual job, which is what?
storyboard.concreteVisual: Text-only question card.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Asks the question the next beat answers.
storyboard.addedInformation: Sets up the answer.

storyboard.claim: The job is managing the ecosystem: assess the fire chief, provide water pressure and resources, manage the perimeter.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Text-only list of three responsibilities.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Answers the question with a list.
storyboard.addedInformation: Names the three duties of the leader in the metaphor.

image.subject: Bill Campbell, a stocky white-haired man in his sixties, warm and direct, wearing a plain open-collar shirt and a sport jacket, stands back with his hands in his pockets as a young engineer types at a desk with two monitors in a glass-walled office at night

storyboard.claim: Pushing the fire chief aside undermines the team architecture you built.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The coach stands back while the engineer keeps working at the desk.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Continues the fire-chief metaphor from the previous beat.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the manager stepping back from the technical work.

image.subject: a young engineer alone at a whiteboard covered in system diagrams, looking at an unsolved problem, while a chair across the room sits empty

storyboard.claim: If the manager always swoops in, the team never learns to step up.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A lone engineer at a whiteboard with no one to hand the problem to.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Follows the step-back metaphor with its cost.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the team left without a chance to take over.

image.subject: three engineers working together at a whiteboard in an open office, while Bill Campbell, a stocky white-haired man in his sixties in a sport jacket, sits back in a chair with arms folded, watching them

storyboard.claim: A builder of teams steps back and lets the trained team operate.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The coach watches quietly as the team solves the problem alone.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Resolves the previous beat by showing the step-back in practice.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the team operating on its own.

image.subject: Bill Campbell, a stocky white-haired man in his sixties, warm and direct, wearing a sport jacket, stands in the doorway of a bright glass conference room about to walk in

storyboard.claim: The last element of Campbell's playbook is the unexpected one.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The coach at a conference room door, about to enter.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Turns from the perimeter lesson to a new section.
storyboard.addedInformation: Introduces Campbell as the subject of the last element.

storyboard.claim: The playbook so far is strict rules, firing, humility and process.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A four-item list of the earlier lessons.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Recaps the earlier parts of the playbook.
storyboard.addedInformation: Lists the hard-edged lessons before the emotional one.

image.subject: Bill Campbell, a stocky white-haired man in his sixties in a sport jacket, rests a hand on the shoulder of Larry Page, a young man in his late twenties with tousled brown hair and a casual sweater, both smiling in a bright office

storyboard.claim: The glue holding high-pressure business together is emotional.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The coach's hand on a young founder's shoulder in a warm moment.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Pivots from the list of hard rules to the emotional glue.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the coach and a founder in a warm, personal moment.

image.subject: a quiet hospital room at dusk, a pale window with soft light, an empty bed with a folded blanket and a wooden chair beside it

storyboard.claim: Steve Jobs is near the end of his life and severely incapacitated.
storyboard.concreteVisual: An empty hospital room with a bed and a chair at dusk.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Introduces the illness that frames the emotional lesson.
storyboard.addedInformation: Sets a quiet hospital setting without showing the patient.

storyboard.claim: Despite the chaos of the tech world, the stakes are huge.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A three-item list of the pressures.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Sets the chaos against the hospital setting.
storyboard.addedInformation: Lists the pressures Campbell still carried.

image.subject: a crowded tech boardroom with a wooden table covered in laptops, papers and phones, a projector screen glowing at the far end

storyboard.claim: Campbell advised many companies at once in a busy world.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A boardroom table covered in laptops and papers.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Continues the chaos beat with a place.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the busy boardroom world of his advisory work.

image.subject: Bill Campbell, a stocky white-haired man in his sixties in a plain open-collar shirt, sits in a plain chair beside a hospital bed, leaning forward with his forearms on his knees and listening quietly, the bed's occupant out of frame

storyboard.claim: Campbell visits his sick friend in a hospital room, not once a month but regularly.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The coach sitting beside a hospital bed, listening.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Shows the coach placed in the hospital setting from the previous beat.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows Campbell personally present with the sick friend.

image.subject: a wall calendar in an office with a neat ring drawn around today's date, a sport jacket hanging on a hook beside a door

storyboard.claim: Showing up every day is the ultimate lesson of the playbook.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A calendar with today circled and a jacket on a hook.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Turns the hospital visit into a daily habit.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the habit of daily presence through a calendar.

left.label: WORK

right.label: LIFE
right.subject: a father at a kitchen table helping a child with homework

storyboard.claim: Corporate life tries to wall off work from personal life, but you cannot separate them.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A side-by-side of a spreadsheet desk and a family kitchen table.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Sets up the claim that the professional and personal cannot be separated.
storyboard.addedInformation: Contrasts the two worlds the corporate wall tries to split.

storyboard.claim: The idea of purely rational economic actors is a lie.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Text-only punchline.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Answers the wall-between-work-and-life claim.
storyboard.addedInformation: Rejects the rational-actor myth outright.

image.subject: a manager in her thirties with shoulder-length brown hair and a cardigan, sitting across a desk from a colleague, leaning in to listen

storyboard.claim: To build trust you have to care about people, which requires vulnerability.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A manager leaning in to listen across a desk.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Follows the lie with the positive version.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the vulnerable listening the claim describes.

storyboard.claim: The job is not only tracking OKRs.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A three-item checklist of what managers do.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Introduces the OKR work the next beats contrast against.
storyboard.addedInformation: Defines OKRs as the logical goals managers track.

image.subject: a laptop showing a bar chart left open on a desk, while beside it a manager and a team member share a cup of coffee and talk

storyboard.claim: Any software can track OKRs; the manager provides the human element.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A laptop chart on the desk beside two people talking over coffee.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Contrasts the software from the checklist with the human element.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the human side that the software cannot provide.

storyboard.claim: The manager's task is to legitimize empathy within the organization.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Text-only quotation of the principle.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: States the principle the human element serves.
storyboard.addedInformation: Names the principle directly.

image.subject: Bill Campbell, a stocky white-haired man in his sixties in a sport jacket, and a young engineer sit on a park bench outside an office, talking relaxedly about their families

storyboard.claim: Ask people about their lives and their families, and know what stresses them.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The coach and an engineer chatting on a park bench.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Gives the principle a concrete action.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the personal conversation the claim describes.

image.subject: a closed laptop with a spreadsheet pushed to the edge of a desk, and a sport jacket draped over a chair

storyboard.claim: When life gets rough, drop the targets and show up for people.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A pushed-aside spreadsheet and a jacket on a chair.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Follows the personal conversation with the act of putting work aside.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the spreadsheet set aside.

image.subject: a hospital corridor with soft lights and a window at the end, a man in a jacket walking toward a room with a worried expression

storyboard.claim: An executive named Mary Baker was hospitalized while travelling on business.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A hospital corridor with a worried man walking toward a room.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Moves from the principle to a real corporate story.
storyboard.addedInformation: Places the story in a hospital on a business trip.

left.label: FLOWERS
left.subject: a bouquet of flowers on a hospital tray table with a small card

right.label: PRIVATE JET
right.subject: a sleek private jet cabin with leather seats and a small window

storyboard.claim: The normal response would be flowers; Campbell chartered a private jet.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Flowers on the left, a private jet cabin on the right.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Sets the normal response against the extraordinary one.
storyboard.addedInformation: Contrasts the ordinary gesture with the jet.

image.subject: a husband in a light jacket sitting beside a hospital bed holding his wife's hand, a sunlit window behind them

storyboard.claim: The husband was flown to be with his wife and to bring her home comfortably.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A husband holding his wife's hand beside a hospital bed.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Shows the result of the jet from the previous beat.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the husband at her side in the hospital.

image.subject: a group of employees in an open-plan office gathered in a loose circle, listening to one another and talking, some with coffee cups

storyboard.claim: The act sends a shock wave through the whole company.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Employees gathered in a loose circle, talking together.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Moves from the single gesture to its effect on the company.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the wider company hearing the story.

image.subject: a group of employees in a bright office standing close together, one of them a woman in a cardigan, all listening intently to a speaker out of frame

storyboard.claim: Employees see that leaders are devoted to them as human beings, not line items.

storyboard.relationToPrevious: Extends the effect to every employee who hears the story.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the audience of employees who hear the story.

storyboard.claim: This generates loyalty that no bonus or stock option could buy.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Text-only stat.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Concludes the loyalty effect of the gesture.
storyboard.addedInformation: Compares loyalty to bonuses and stock options.

storyboard.claim: The listener may ask how a middle manager could do this.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Text-only question.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Raises the objection the next beats answer.
storyboard.addedInformation: Frames the question about scale.

image.subject: a sleek white private jet on a tarmac at dusk beside a glass corporate tower

storyboard.claim: The grand gestures seem reserved for the ultra rich with big budgets.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A private jet at dusk beside a glass tower.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Answers the question with the luxury view.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the wealth the objection assumes.

image.subject: a crowded Boston bar with college graduates raising glasses around a long wooden counter, a warm evening crowd

storyboard.claim: Campbell bought out whole bars for college graduates.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A crowded bar with graduates raising glasses.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Adds the second grand gesture to the luxury view.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the bar gesture for graduates.

image.subject: a middle manager at a cluttered desk with a stack of expense forms and a calculator, looking thoughtful under office lights

storyboard.claim: A middle manager has a frozen budget and a tiny expense account.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A manager at a cluttered desk with expense forms.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Turns the luxury view to the ordinary manager.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the tight budget the manager works with.

storyboard.claim: Is this just billionaire empathy that does not apply to everyone else?
storyboard.concreteVisual: Text-only question.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Restates the objection as the core question.
storyboard.addedInformation: Frames the central question for the ordinary manager.

image.subject: a pile of coins blurred in the foreground while a manager leans toward a colleague in sharp focus across a desk

storyboard.claim: The scale of money does not matter; the scale of attention does.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Blurred coins in front, a sharp manager leaning in.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Answers the core question with the key idea.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows attention as the thing that matters more than money.

storyboard.claim: You do not need a private jet to prove you care.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Text-only quotation.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Names the key idea from the previous beat.
storyboard.addedInformation: States that attention proves care.

image.subject: Bill Campbell, a stocky white-haired man in his sixties in a sport jacket, leans forward at a conference table with his hands raised mid-clap while colleagues turn toward him in a glass-walled office

storyboard.relationToPrevious: Introduces the clap as the concrete example of attention.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the clap in a routine meeting.

image.subject: close-up of several pairs of hands clapping above a laptop in a meeting room, a notebook open on the table

storyboard.claim: Five loud percussive claps in the meeting.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Close-up of hands clapping over a laptop.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Zooms in on the clap from the previous beat.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the clapping as a visible gesture.

storyboard.claim: A manager named Klay Beavor institutionalized the clap in his own team.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A three-item list of the spread of the habit.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Shows the clap spreading beyond Campbell.
storyboard.addedInformation: Names the manager who adopted the clap.

image.subject: a team lead in a bright open office giving a high five to a colleague at a standing desk, a few teammates smiling nearby

storyboard.claim: Recognition is democratized and costs nothing to give.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A high five at a standing desk among smiling teammates.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Generalizes the clap into everyday recognition.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows recognition given by anyone on the team.

storyboard.claim: It costs zero dollars to remember a child's name and ask about their tournament.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Text-only stat.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Lists zero-cost gestures of attention.
storyboard.addedInformation: Gives the zero-dollar cost of attention.

image.subject: a manager in her thirties with shoulder-length brown hair and a cardigan quietly standing beside a junior employee's desk, speaking softly after a meeting

storyboard.claim: Noticing a quiet junior employee and checking on them costs nothing.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A manager speaking softly beside a junior employee's desk.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Gives a second zero-cost example.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the one-on-one check-in.

storyboard.claim: Compassion is hyperfocused, undivided attention.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Text-only quotation.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Defines the compassion behind the jet and the clap.
storyboard.addedInformation: Names the core of the compassion.

image.subject: a team gathered around a long wooden conference table in a bright room, the coach at the head with his hands clasped, relaxed and attentive

storyboard.claim: Trust between founders and managers is the secret sauce.

storyboard.relationToPrevious: Closes the section on attention as the tool for trust.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the team trust the section describes.

storyboard.relationToPrevious: Closes the previous passage on the jet and the compassion of focused attention.

storyboard.relationToPrevious: Turns from praise of the method to a critical examination.

storyboard.relationToPrevious: Continues the turn to criticism.

image.subject: a printed playbook manuscript spread across a desk with handwritten red pen marks in the margins, beside a closed laptop in a bright office

storyboard.claim: We have to raise the essential criticism of the trillion-dollar coach philosophy.

storyboard.relationToPrevious: Follows the structural flaw statement with the act of critique.
storyboard.addedInformation: Frames the critique as an editorial review of the playbook itself.

image.subject: a dog-eared paperback book lying open on a glass-topped office desk beside a coffee mug, a pen resting in the gutter of the pages

image.subject: a stocky white-haired man in his sixties, warm and direct, wearing a plain open-collar shirt and a sport jacket, the posture of a football coach, sitting quietly in the back row of a staff meeting while a man in his fifties with short graying hair and a dark blazer over an open-collar shirt, measured and attentive, speaks at the head of a glass-walled office conference table

storyboard.claim: Campbell acted as the oracle, sitting in the back of Schmidt's staff meetings.

image.subject: a stocky white-haired man in his sixties, warm and direct, wearing a plain open-collar shirt and a sport jacket, the posture of a football coach, walking a younger executive aside down a bright office hallway, one hand resting on the younger man's shoulder

storyboard.relationToPrevious: Details the oracle's methods from the previous beat.
storyboard.addedInformation: Describes the hallway smoothing done in person.

storyboard.claim: He filled the communication gaps and broke ties with emotional intelligence; he was the magic ingredient.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Text-led statement on the single person holding the system together.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Sums up the oracle's role.
storyboard.addedInformation: Names the emotional intelligence that the system depended on.

storyboard.claim: What happens when a company scales from 500 people to 10,000 or 100,000 employees?
storyboard.concreteVisual: A real question set as text, the shape of the question is the point.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Turns the single-person dependence into the scaling question.
storyboard.addedInformation: Gives the concrete scale numbers at which the method is tested.

image.subject: an empty chair at the head of a long wooden boardroom table, a dark projector screen behind it and rows of unoccupied chairs in a tech company conference room

storyboard.claim: Campbell cannot physically be in the room to read the body language.
storyboard.concreteVisual: An empty chair at the head of the table where the coach would have sat.
storyboard.onScreenText: HE CANNOT BE IN THE ROOM
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Answers the scaling question with an empty seat.
storyboard.addedInformation: Visualises the absence of the one person who read the room.

storyboard.claim: A culture built on one man's hypercalibrated gut judgment breaks down.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Text-led statement; the collapse is an idea, not a picture.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Gives the verdict on the scaling question.
storyboard.addedInformation: States the fragility of a culture built on one person.

image.subject: a woman in her thirties with shoulder-length brown hair and a cardigan, sitting across a desk from a colleague, studying the colleague's face with a quiet, watchful expression in a bright office

storyboard.claim: Innate intuition cannot be systemized or turned into an algorithm.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A manager reading a colleague's face across a desk.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Explains why the gut judgment is fragile.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the intuition being exercised, the thing that resists systemizing.

image.subject: a stocky white-haired man in his sixties, warm and direct, wearing a plain open-collar shirt and a sport jacket, the posture of a football coach, giving a younger founder in a dark tee a firm bear hug in a bright startup office

storyboard.claim: Campbell manufactured an envelope of trust by walking in and giving someone a bear hug; relying on a guru is dangerous.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Campbell embracing a younger founder in an office.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Describes the personal trust that cannot be replicated.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the physical, personal gesture behind the trust.

image.subject: a man in his fifties with short dark hair and a light blazer, engaged and conversational, presenting before a projector screen in a glass-walled conference room while one executive in the front row frowns faintly

storyboard.claim: The structure depends on a genius noticing a VP is slightly annoyed during a presentation.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A presenter with one executive in the front row showing a faint irritation.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Gives an everyday example of the guru's attention.
storyboard.addedInformation: Illustrates the subtle cues the guru must catch.

storyboard.claim: The structure will collapse the second the guru retires or, in Bill's case, passes away.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Text punchline; the collapse is the claim, the beat lands on the word.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Completes the guru-dependence argument.
storyboard.addedInformation: Sets up the personal stake of the coach's death.

image.subject: an empty desk by a sunlit office window with a folded sport jacket draped over the back of the chair and a closed notebook on the desk

storyboard.claim: Bill Campbell passed away, so the structure must outlive him.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A quiet empty desk with his jacket, a symbol of absence rather than a depiction of death.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Turns the collapse argument to Campbell's own death.
storyboard.addedInformation: Frames the absence as the reason to build systems.

storyboard.claim: Can this playbook be scaled by average everyday managers who are stressed, tired and not naturally gifted empaths?
storyboard.concreteVisual: A real question set as text, the shape of the question carries it.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Brings the listener into the question.
storyboard.addedInformation: Defines the audience of the test: ordinary managers.

image.subject: a woman in her thirties with shoulder-length brown hair and a cardigan, sitting across a desk from a colleague, looking tired and stressed, rubbing her eyes beside a stack of papers in a late-evening office

storyboard.claim: The system may require emotional intelligence most people do not have.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A tired manager at a desk, the everyday reader the method must work for.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Makes the everyday manager concrete.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the stress of the typical manager the system must serve.

image.subject: a whiteboard covered in a neat grid of boxes and arrows showing meeting cadences and reporting lines, a marker tray below it in a glass-walled Silicon Valley office

storyboard.claim: You cannot clone Campbell, but you can institutionalize the frameworks and structures he used.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A whiteboard grid of structures and cadences.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Answers the test with a structural solution.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the frameworks as a visible structure any team can build.

image.subject: a team of four seated around a conference table on a Monday afternoon, a manager in a cardigan reading a printed trip report aloud while colleagues listen in a bright office

storyboard.claim: You can mandate Monday 1pm trip reports so people connect as humans before fighting over budgets.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A Monday afternoon team meeting around a table with a printed report.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Gives a concrete example of an institutionalized framework.
storyboard.addedInformation: Names the specific Monday 1pm ritual.

storyboard.claim: Enforce the rule that managers speak last, and standardize whiteboard one-on-ones led by the employee.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Two-item text list of the enforced rules.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Continues the list of institutional rules.
storyboard.addedInformation: Specifies two concrete rules for meetings.

image.subject: a woman in her thirties with shoulder-length brown hair and a cardigan, sitting across a desk from a colleague, listening with her chin in her hand while the colleague points to a whiteboard agenda

storyboard.claim: The employee leads the agenda, forcing the manager to listen rather than dictate, which hacks empathy.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A manager listening while the employee leads from a whiteboard agenda.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Shows the rule being applied in practice.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the power reversal in a one-on-one.

image.subject: a whiteboard in a tech office with a rigid grid of meeting slots drawn in black marker, a clean desk and a hand holding the marker at the corner

storyboard.claim: You cannot guarantee brilliant empaths, but you can build a rigid system that requires them to act like one.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A rigid meeting grid on a whiteboard, the scaffold that substitutes for innate empathy.
storyboard.onScreenText: A SYSTEM THAT ACTS LIKE ONE
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Summarises the institutional answer.
storyboard.addedInformation: Frames the system as a substitute for innate empathy.

storyboard.claim: Why does it matter?
storyboard.concreteVisual: A real question set as text, the shape of the question carries it.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Opens the payoff on why the analysis matters.
storyboard.addedInformation: Sets up the payoff question.

image.subject: a stocky white-haired man in his sixties, warm and direct, wearing a plain open-collar shirt and a sport jacket, the posture of a football coach, holding a football in a tech office while an engineer's desk with two monitors and a code editor sits beside him

storyboard.claim: Campbell was not the greatest coach because he wrote elegant C++ or designed hardware.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Campbell with a football next to an engineer's desk, showing he was not a technologist.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Turns the payoff to what Campbell actually was.
storyboard.addedInformation: Contrasts Campbell with the technical craft of the companies.

image.subject: two engineers at a workstation with two monitors showing a code editor, one leaning back in his chair to talk across the desk to the other in a bright Silicon Valley office

storyboard.claim: He knew the industry was utterly obsessed with what is being built.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Two engineers at a workstation, the building obsession.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Continues the payoff with the industry's obsession.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the building obsession as a workstation scene.

image.subject: a product launch stage in front of a dark auditorium, a glowing demo screen behind a podium with a single spotlight on it

storyboard.claim: The thing that is built only determines success in the short run; long-term success depends elsewhere.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A product launch stage with a lit demo screen.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Sets up the contrast between product and people.
storyboard.addedInformation: Visualises the product side of the equation.

image.subject: a stocky white-haired man in his sixties, warm and direct, wearing a plain open-collar shirt and a sport jacket, the posture of a football coach, and a man in his fifties with short graying hair and a dark blazer over an open-collar shirt, measured and attentive, leaning toward each other across a conference table and shaking hands

storyboard.claim: Long-term success depends on who is building it and whether they trust the person beside them.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Campbell and Schmidt shaking hands across a table, trust made visible.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Makes the people side of the argument concrete.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows two cast members building trust together.

image.subject: a team of five gathered around a whiteboard in a bright office, everyone standing at eye level and listening to a colleague who is pointing at a diagram

storyboard.claim: The playbook is about making everyone else in the room feel legendary, not about the leader.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A team at eye level around a whiteboard, everyone equal in the room.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Redirects the legend from the leader to the team.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the team, not the leader, as the focus.

image.subject: a slim man in his forties with a black mock turtleneck, jeans and sneakers, intense focused gaze, standing at a glass-walled office window with arms crossed

storyboard.claim: Think of the most difficult genius on your team right now.
storyboard.concreteVisual: An intense, difficult genius standing at a window, the person the reader is asked to picture.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Asks the listener to picture a specific person.
storyboard.addedInformation: Gives the listener a concrete person to think about.

image.subject: a quiet young engineer with head down at a workstation with two monitors and a code editor, focused and diligent in a bright office late in the afternoon

storyboard.claim: Now think about the quietest, most diligent worker you manage.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A quiet diligent engineer at a workstation, the person easily overlooked.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Pairs the difficult genius with the quiet worker.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the diligent worker the reader is asked to notice.

image.subject: a manager in a cardigan walking through a glass office door at sunrise with a coffee cup in hand, the horizon glowing pale over the Silicon Valley hills outside

storyboard.claim: Tomorrow, ask what invisible gap of trust exists between you and your team, and what you will do to fill it.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A manager entering the office at sunrise, the morning the reader is asked to act on.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Closes the chapter with a call to act tomorrow.
storyboard.addedInformation: Ends with the concrete question the reader takes into the office.
